title: What makes a deed valid
body: A valid deed needs a competent grantor, an identifiable grantee, words of conveyance, a legal description, the grantor's signature, and delivery and acceptance. Notarizing (acknowledgment) is needed to record, not to be valid.
example: A Reno grantor signs and hands a deed to the buyer at closing. Title passes on delivery.
hook: Signed, delivered, accepted: title moves.

title: Deed types and recording
body: General warranty gives the most protection. Special warranty covers only the grantor's ownership. Grant deeds carry limited implied warranties. Quitclaims give none. Recording gives constructive notice to the world.
example: A divorcing Henderson couple uses a quitclaim so one spouse releases any interest.
hook: General guards it all. Quitclaim guards nothing.

title: Searching title
body: A title search traces the chain of title through public records. An abstract summarizes what's recorded. Gaps, unreleased liens or bad signatures are clouds that may need a quiet title action.
example: A Carson City title search finds a 1998 lien never released. The seller clears it before closing.
hook: Follow the chain; fix the breaks.

title: Title insurance
body: Title insurance covers losses from covered defects that existed before the policy date, like forged deeds. A lender's policy protects only the lender. An owner's policy protects the buyer.
example: A Las Vegas buyer who bought an owner's policy is covered when a forged deed from 2005 surfaces.
hook: Lender's policy protects the lender. Buy your own.

title: Escrow and closing
body: An escrow agent is a neutral party who holds money and documents and follows the parties' written instructions. At closing, each party's debits and credits are settled, the deed is recorded, and funds are paid out.
example: Escrow companies commonly handle closings in Nevada.
hook: Escrow: neutral hands, written instructions.

title: Prorations and tax reporting
body: Prorating splits ongoing costs by the days each party owns the property. The closing agent usually reports the sale on Form 1099-S. When the seller is a foreign person, FIRPTA may require the buyer to withhold part of the price.
example: A Canadian seller of a Mesquite condo has FIRPTA withholding taken at closing unless an exemption applies.
hook: Split it by days; report it to the IRS.

title: Foreclosure and alternatives
body: Judicial foreclosure goes through court. Nonjudicial foreclosure uses a trustee's sale under a deed of trust. Alternatives include a short sale, where the lender accepts less, or a deed in lieu. Unsold properties become REO.
example: A Las Vegas lender approves a short sale for less than the loan balance.
hook: Short sale: the lender takes less.

title: Involuntary transfers and taxes
body: Adverse possession transfers title after open, continuous, hostile, exclusive use for the period the law sets. Probate passes property by will or by law. A 1031 exchange defers tax on investment property. The home sale exclusion shields gain on a main home.
example: A Reno couple sells the home they lived in for 6 years with $300,000 gain and owes no federal tax on it.
hook: OCHE: open, continuous, hostile, exclusive.

title: The property manager's job
body: A property manager is a general agent under a management agreement. The job: set rents, market and lease units, screen tenants fairly, collect rent, maintain the property, budget, and report to the owner.
example: A Henderson manager runs a 24-unit complex for an out-of-state owner.
hook: Protect the property, maximize the income.

title: Maintenance and risk
body: Preventive maintenance heads off problems. Corrective maintenance fixes them. Managers handle risk four ways: avoid, control, transfer (usually with insurance), or retain.
example: A Reno manager schedules furnace service every fall so there are fewer winter breakdowns.
hook: Avoid, control, transfer, retain.

title: Lease types
body: Gross lease: tenant pays fixed rent, owner pays expenses. Net lease: tenant also pays some or all expenses. Percentage lease: retail base rent plus a share of sales. Ground lease: long-term lease of land.
example: A Las Vegas Strip retailer pays base rent plus 6% of sales over a set amount.
hook: Gross: owner pays. Net: tenant pays more.

title: Assignment vs. sublease
body: In an assignment, the tenant transfers the whole remaining lease, and the new tenant deals with the landlord directly. In a sublease, the original tenant rents to a subtenant and stays responsible to the landlord.
example: A Reno tenant subleases a room for the summer and remains liable for all the rent.
hook: Sublease: you're still on the hook.

title: Tenant rights
body: Tenants have the right to quiet enjoyment and a habitable home. If the landlord's failure makes the place unusable, it's constructive eviction. Landlords can't evict in retaliation for complaints.
example: A Las Vegas landlord ignores a broken AC in July for weeks. The tenant may have a constructive eviction claim.
hook: Habitable, quiet, and no payback evictions.

title: Deposits and evictions
body: Security deposits are held for the tenant and returned less lawful deductions within the time state law sets. Landlords must use the court eviction process; changing locks or removing belongings themselves is not allowed.
example: A Henderson landlord files for eviction through the court instead of changing the locks.
hook: Evict through court, not the hardware store.

title: Commission and splits
body: Commission = sale price × rate. Then split it in steps: first between brokerages, then between each broker and salesperson. Read every word: "of the commission" isn't "of the price."
example: A $400,000 Henderson sale at 5% is $20,000; split 50/50 between brokerages is $10,000 each.
hook: Price times rate, then split, then split again.

title: Seller's net and working backward
body: Seller's net = price − commission − costs − loan payoff. To find the price a seller needs, add the net and costs, then divide by (1 − commission rate).
example: A Reno seller wants $380,000 after a 5% commission and $5,000 costs: (380,000 + 5,000) ÷ 0.95 ≈ $405,263.
hook: Need a net? Divide by what's left after commission.

title: Prorating step by step
body: Find the daily (or monthly) amount, count the days owed, and multiply. Know whether the exam uses a 360-day year with 30-day months, or a 365-day year. Decide who owes whom.
example: Annual taxes of $3,600 on a 360-day year are $10 a day.
hook: Daily amount × days owed.

title: Who gets the credit
body: Taxes paid in arrears: the seller owes the buyer for the days the seller owned the home, so it's a seller debit and buyer credit. Rent collected in advance: the seller owes the buyer for the days after closing.
example: A Las Vegas seller collected June rent. Closing is June 20, so the buyer is credited for the rest of June.
hook: Whoever used it or kept it pays for it.

title: Interest and amortization
body: Interest = principal × rate × time. For a monthly payment, annual interest ÷ 12 gives the first month's interest; the rest of the payment reduces principal. Early payments are mostly interest.
example: On a $300,000 loan at 6%, the first month's interest is $1,500.
hook: Annual interest ÷ 12, then the rest hits principal.

title: PITI and ratios
body: PITI is principal, interest, taxes and insurance. Lenders compare PITI to gross monthly income (housing ratio) and total debts to income (debt ratio).
example: A Reno borrower's PITI is $2,240 on $8,000 monthly income: a 28% housing ratio.
hook: PITI over income.

title: IRV for investments
body: Income = Rate × Value. Cover the one you want: Value = Income ÷ Rate; Rate = Income ÷ Value. Use net operating income, not gross, unless the question says otherwise.
example: A Henderson duplex with $30,000 NOI bought for $500,000 earns a 6% cap rate.
hook: IRV: cover what you need.

title: Percent change
body: Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old. Appreciation uses the original value as the base. Profit percentage uses the original cost as the base.
example: A Reno home bought for $350,000 sells for $420,000: a 20% gain.
hook: Change over original.

title: Area and acreage
body: Rectangle: length × width. Triangle: ½ × base × height. One acre is 43,560 sq ft; one square yard is 9 sq ft. Convert units before multiplying.
example: A 150 × 290.4 ft lot in Pahrump is 43,560 sq ft, exactly one acre.
hook: 43,560 makes an acre; 9 makes a yard.

title: Front feet and volume
body: Front feet measure the side facing the street; it's listed first in lot dimensions. Volume = length × width × height. Cubic yards = cubic feet ÷ 27.
example: A 60 × 120 Henderson lot priced at $2,000 per front foot costs $120,000.
hook: Front first; 27 cubic feet in a cubic yard.

title: Property tax math
body: Tax = assessed value × tax rate. Rates may be in percent, per $100, or in mills (per $1,000). Convert the rate to a decimal before multiplying.
hook: Per hundred, divide by 100; per mill, by 1,000.

title: Transfer tax math
body: Transfer tax is usually a rate per $500 or per $1,000 of price, or a percentage. Divide the price into units, round as the law requires, and multiply. Nevada's rate and rules are covered in the state units.
hook: Count the units, then multiply.
